newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin stable, talks to leaders by phone.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin stable, talks to leaders by phone.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin was receiving treatment for pneumonia in hospital on Friday and managing affairs of state by telephone, but his new illness plunged Russia into a new bout of political anxiety.

The Kremlin described Yeltsin's condition as stable some 24 hours after the 65-year-old president was admitted to the elite Central Clinical Hospital in Moscow on Wednesday evening -- less than two months after undergoing multiple heart bypass surgery.
No new bulletins on his condition were forthcoming early on Friday.
Russian television said he had already been in contact by telephone with a number of Russian and foreign leaders. It said he might speak to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl later in the day.
Kohl told reporters in Bonn on Thursday that Yeltsin was alert and he planned to speak to him, particularly to persuade Moscow to accept NATO's expansion eastward.

The Kremlin has played down Yeltsin's condition and insists it has nothing to do with last November's quintuple heart bypass operation. Doctors who examined him on Thursday found no deterioration in his condition.

Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Yeltsin's constitutional deputy, was confident enough to begin a planned week's holiday near Moscow. He spoke by telephone to Yeltsin, who is being treated with antibiotics.

Chernomyrdin, who would take power for up to three months before elections if the president had to step down, spent six months effectively running the country after Yeltsin suffered a bout of heart trouble shortly before his re-election on July 3.
But the prime minister held formal power for just a day when Yeltsin had his operation on November 5. The president returned to work only on December 23.
NTV television said arrangements had been made for the Kremlin leader to control Russia's nuclear arsenal from hospital.

General Alexander Lebed, whom Yeltsin sacked as national security adviser two weeks before his heart operation for overtly pursuing his own ambitions during the president's last illness, immediately called on him to quit.
"The president is badly ill," he said. "No one is dealing with the economy...Someone has to rule."

The tough-talking Lebed, voted Man of the Year in a Russian opinion poll last month, would be a strong contender in any snap election. Chernomyrdin would probably be the choice of the Moscow establishment, but Lebed has much wider popular appeal.
It is not clear how long Yeltsin may be in hospital.

The heart surgeon who performed November's operation, Renat Akchurin, and U.S. specialist Michael DeBakey, who advised him, both stressed that the president's convalescence from surgery had gone well and saw no link to the pneumonia.
But some international heart experts said it was possible that Yeltsin -- who looked frail during a meeting last Saturday with Kohl -- could be seriously ill.

Izvestia columnist Stepan Kiselyov, in an editorial in Friday's issue of the liberal daily headlined "President Sick, Premier On Holiday, Country All On Its Own", detected a similar pattern to last year in the way the Kremlin press office's early optimism was later seen to belie a more serious illness.

Some political analysts say Russia has proved it can maintain a measure of stability without Yeltsin in the Kremlin. Chernomyrdin and the president's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais have ample powers to run the country.
But their in-fighting with Lebed and others last year raised fears of instability and criticism that Russia's deep social and economic problems were not being properly addressed.

"It means, ultimately, continuing that period of terrible stagnation, when not one senior official will be able to take a single decision of even minimal responsibility and which the Russian economy desperately needs today...," Kiselyov wrote.
